generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy based on CoCrFeMnNi, processed to develop a hierarchical FCC microstructure with tailored nanoscale precipitate dispersion, will exhibit improved ductility compared to its conventionally processed counterpart.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or conventionally processed state displaying typical ductility limitations.
generation.intervention: Apply a multi-step thermal/mechanical treatment designed to refine the grain size and induce a controlled dispersion of nanoscale secondary (precipitate) phases within a predominantly FCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures relevant to real service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Hierarchical microstructure featuring a stable FCC matrix with uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates and refined grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The FCC structure provides abundant slip systems for plastic deformation, while the nanoscale precipitates help modulate dislocation motion. This combination alleviates dislocation pile-up, reducing local stress concentrations and thus enhancing ductility without severely compromising strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed CoCrFeMnNi alloy is expected to show a higher ductility (greater percentage elongation to failure) while maintaining or slightly improving its strength relative to the untreated state.
generation.baseline: The untreated or conventionally processed CoCrFeMnNi alloy, which typically exhibits lower ductility due to less controlled microstructure.
generation.boundary: The expected improvement is contingent upon precise control of processing parameters; extreme service conditions or improper processing may not yield the desired microstructural control and ductility enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in ductility are subject to variability in processing conditions and potential trade-offs with strength, pending further experimental verification.

Characterize the microstructures using TEM and XRD, and perform room temperature and moderately elevated temperature tensile tests on both sets.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in ductility (i.e., higher percentage elongation) along with confirmed microstructural modifications (refined grains and nanoscale precipitate dispersion) compared to the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

decision.trend: Over several studies on high-entropy alloys (HEAs), researchers have pursued enhanced ductility by tuning composition, microstructure, and processing history. Early attempts often produced strong, brittle materials in high-temperature alloys (e.g., some refractory compositions), but subsequent work introduced strategies to improve ductility, such as stabilizing an FCC phase (notably in CoCrFeMnNi) or engineering multiple coherent precipitates in duplex structures. More recently, stepwise thermo-mechanical processing, selective laser melting, or high-pressure high-temperature treatments have each been applied to refine grain boundaries, form nanoscale secondary phases, and suppress brittle fracture, thereby increasing ductility at room and elevated temperatures. Despite these advances, the trade-off between strength and ductility remains a key challenge, especially under extreme service conditions or at very high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: Although multiple-phase architectures and advanced processing routes have raised ductility significantly, it remains difficult to achieve consistently high ductility together with superior strength under both ambient and high-temperature conditions. Balancing phase stability, grain refinement, and interfacial strengthening without incurring embrittlement is still an open challenge for many of these new alloys.
decision.lever: Design a hierarchical, predominantly FCC microstructure with tailored secondary phase dispersion (e.g., nanoscale precipitates), carefully controlling grain size and interface density via multi-step thermal/mechanical treatments
decision.why: FCC-based HEAs (like CoCrFeMnNi and related blends) exhibit substantial ductility due to abundant slip systems, but can lose strength if not carefully managed. Based on the latest trends in refining grain structures and precipitate distributions, tuning the microstructure to retain a stable FCC matrix while introducing ductile secondary features offers a straightforward path to improve both ductility and strength, in line with the incremental successes reported in the literature for high-performance materials.
